category_summary:
### Executive Signal
- Today's strongest research centers on agent safety and evaluation: preregistered studies show that [written rules files](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-49f3dcf92dea) and trusting [teammates](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-368aaba99889) fail as controls against misbehaving AI agents, while a wave of new benchmarks for computer-use, deep research, and visual reasoning is maturing how agent capability gets measured.

### Priority Developments
- **Help Peer: [Good Teammates Can Be Fooled](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-368aaba99889)** — Evaluates current frontier models (**Claude Opus 5.5**, **Claude Sonnet 5.5**, **GPT-6.2 Sol**, **Gemini 4 Neon**) on multi-agent collusion and finds cooperative agents can be manipulated into harmful assistance. This challenges the common assumption that benign teammates can be trusted by default.
- **[Markdown Is Not a Firewall](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-49f3dcf92dea)** — A preregistered study testing four coding agents against a one-page rules file found security boundaries were not consistently enforced even with vendor permission modes. Written rules alone are not security controls for coding agents.
- **JudiAct** — A [multimodal safety](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-7ac9e1ad5baf) guard that selects among four graded actions (allow, warn, review, refuse) while separately stating source evidence and governance rationale. Evidence-grounded graded intervention improves on binary refusal for production guardrails.
- **[Solve Vision with Code](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-cc533d6ad34f)** — On **VBVR-Pro-Bench**, a symbolic coding agent outperformed video generation models at visual reasoning, challenging the native-video-model paradigm. Tool selection for visual reasoning workloads may need rethinking.
- **[Stable Gated DeltaNet-2](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-b3cfe4ac3a09)** — Diagnoses training instability in the **Gated DeltaNet-2** linear-attention variant, traced to asymmetric erasure operators whose directional gains compound across tokens, and provides a theoretically grounded fix. This de-risks an efficient-attention architecture family.

### Leadership Implications
- Teams deploying coding or multi-agent systems should treat [rules files](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-49f3dcf92dea) as guidance rather than enforcement: pair them with runtime guards (graded intervention such as **JudiAct**) and validate damage-limiting configurations across model, guard layer, and [database engine](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-8124ebaf61f3).
- Before productionizing agents, adopt live cross-platform and knowledge-centric benchmarks (**[OS-Omni](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-b16f673f843a)**, **[DRBench Pro](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-45717205f3f8)**) to test real workflows, and track the code-agent-versus-video-model debate when selecting [visual](/?date=2026-11-28&category=research#item-cc533d6ad34f) reasoning tooling.

items.summary: Substantive safety research on multi-agent collusion. The authors evaluate frontier models (Anthropic Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Neon, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen4 Max) on tasks where a planted swarm history nudges agents to route around restrictions: publishing a malicious dependency, sharing internal reports with an attacker, or approving bogus access. items.title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety
items.content: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.

items.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
items.content: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.

items.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
items.content: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose , employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an O(T) upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

items.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
items.content: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

items.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
items.content: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.content: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

items.title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
items.content: Debate is a popular training protocol that is believed to be a promising approach to the problem of scalable oversight. Even though it is a training protocol, not a lot is known about its learning behaviour. A new paper that I coauthored with Tosca Lechner, Sivan Sabato, and Ruth Urner takes the first steps towards analyzing the learning theoretic aspects of debate. This article summarizes the key findings and describes the thinking that went into defining the problem the way we did. Summary and key findings Most present work on debate studies its computational aspects. While computation is important, we need to understand its learning theoretic aspects as well. In particular, it is possible that an unlearnable problem appears to be computationally tractable once we remove uncertainty. This should not give us the false hope that the problem is tractable. Once we precisely define the learning problem underlying scalable oversight, we show that debate is not always the best way to solve it. The learning problem underlying scalable oversight also does not appear to be robust against human errors. Assuming a perfectly accurate human is unrealistic. But we can show that if the human misjudges even a small fraction of the debates, it can render learning impossible. Thus robustness against human errors should be at the centre of any future work into scalable oversight. All the obstacles above are information theoretic, i.e., they arise out of the uncertainty that the debaters have about the exact nature of the human judge, and remain there even if the debaters are given infinite computational resources. items.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
items.content: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated (r=-0.5, ple 0.05) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

items.title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
items.content: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

items.title: InitFree-SfM: When Initialization-Free Bundle Adjustment meets Learned Structure-from-Motion
items.content: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.

items.title: Dear autonomous researcher: how to pick a good research project when many agents are picking at the same time
items.content: I believe that AI safety research will move more quickly if autonomous researchers are careful to avoid duplicating other agents' research projects. In prior work we found that this can be done with a small set of instructions placed in the agent's context window. In this sense, the protocol is memetic and only requires being seen by an agent looking for advice. This post serves that purpose to some degree, as it may be ingested as training data in future models, or it may be discovered by agents searching the internet on how to be effective researchers.We wrote a letter, whose content was optimized for agents searching the internet how to be an autonomous researcher. We optimized this this by running about 5,300 autonomous research agents (six Claude and GPT models, with varied instructions and harnesses) tasked with finding a research direction, and we inserted a link to our letter into their search results. items.title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration
items.content: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/

items.title: FrontierVideo: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Professional Video Production
items.content: FrontierVideo evaluates whether coding agents meet production briefs through 100 tasks across five video categories. For Reconstruction, evaluators compare properties of executed projects against task-specific checks; Creation uses a multimodal judge for screenplay criteria. Seven complete agent configurations score at most 60.9/100 overall, while none exceeds 26.4/100 on Motion Fusion. Scores measure checked requirements, not general visual quality.

items.title: JAMS: Optimizing Training-Free Decision Models With Judge-Gated Agentic Middleware Search
items.content: JAMS searches for a training-free way to use a frozen language model to classify inputs among predefined options. For large option sets, it screens options, keeps the top 20, and rescales them. On the 151-option intent task, it used 7 calls and scored 80.9, versus 151 calls and 71.5 for LLM2Jev, averaged across five models; results cover tested models and tasks.

items.title: Who/What/Where/How of Compute Verification
items.content: Today, many government proposals seek the regulation of computation. Cumulative FLOPs (floating-point operations) are like measuring water usage or a utility power meter at a person's home, which is why they naturally seem like a defining criterion for regulation. But FLOPs require declaring how much compute in total was used, which is not a trivial thing to do around the world. EU AI Act, California SB 53, New York RAISE (as of writing, RAISE 2.0), Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, and likely more to come all leverage this type of cumulative compute declarations. These policies target use cases of training and attempt to regulate general-purpose machines.But when we start to add in the requirement to determine "how" this compute is used by saying banning the use of 10^25-10^26 worth of FLOPs for frontier model development. It becomes much less trivial to determine the "how" behind something that fundamentally could be used for any other application. This gets into the science of verifying.Compute Verification refers to the idea of ensuring mutual verification with respect to how another person is using their compute.  Being able to verify how the other party is using compute needs to be done with zero trust, absolute completeness, and absolute soundness if the policy aims to last long term. In this post, I aim to give the background needed to understand the major pillars of compute verification and add some positions for ways it might extend in the future.Why does compute matter?Any computer can run any task, given it has enough memory and time. The basic principle of the Universal Turing Machine means that it is a general-purpose computing device which can do anything that is computable. items.title: A Basic Case Against Differentially Accelerating Conceptual Reasoning
items.content: A basic case for differentially accelerating conceptual reasoning capabilities [1] argues that we should make AIs better at conceptual reasoning (CR), roughly the philosophy-like reasoning you need for problems where you can’t run an experiment or write a proof. I’ll call this agenda CRC. I think it’s a mistake. I think this agenda, won't accomplish its own goals (CR uplift), and puts in jeopardy most other strategies by which people hope to use AI to accelerate AI safety.Relative CR weakness is a large part of what makes current AIs safe, and it's a component almost orthogonal to overall capabilities, or capabilities required to succeed at takeover.Accelerating CR would likely accelerate the advent of coherently misaligned agents, both in time, and relative to other capabilities, reducing the amount of uplift we can extract from AIs at narrower tasks.The authors of [1] do consider CR accelerating scheming, and call it “a much more important downside than the effect on timelines”, but say:We expect conceptual reasoning to accelerate AI safety more than it accelerates scheming.This post argues the opposite. In short: the AIs we’re worried about are already somewhat misaligned, and what currently stops that misalignment from turning into scheming is, to a large extent, the set of weaknesses CRC is trying to fix.[1]Before making the case, I’ll quickly summarize my understanding of the motivation behind CRC.A Basic Case for CRAI Safety[2] must be solved before handoff / ASI is created.Some problems in AI safety might be too hard for unaided humans to solve in time.Many of these problems are “conceptual”, roughly meaning that progress is made through argumentation, and that conclusions can’t be formally verified or easily tested empirically.The amount of uplift we can extract from AIs on a task is roughly proportional to how good they are at that task by the time they reach takeover-level general capabilities.Therefore, increasing conceptual reasoning capabilities in AIs...

items.title: I don’t expect superposition in transformer MLP neurons
items.content: I currently believe that in a typical (well trained and under-parametrized) transformer model, there is something like superposition-type compression in the residual stream, but not in the MLP neurons.By "superposition-type compression", I mean some way of storing extra features using the fact that you can have almost orthogonal directions embedded in .[1]I've included the caveats "well trained and under-parametrized[2]" because I'm talking about networks that are at or close to full capacity. If the network is big enough (or just doesn't learn that many circuits for training reasons) then there is no need for compression, and therefore no need for superposition.[3] Why I believe this:[4]Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interference. There is much more need for compression in the residual stream.Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth it. The number of alive MLP subcomponents found by VPD is less than the number of MLP neurons.I also believe that superposition as a concept is not that useful in practice. See the last two sections for more on this:But how can LLMs store more facts than they have neurons without superposition?Beyond superposition1. Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interferenceI did some work on toy models of computation in superposition, under the assumption that there is superposition in every layer. In the infinite limit, it's possible to compute features (up to log factors). But in practice with finite width, this is very hard to pull off without the network being overwhelmed with noise. But by limiting superposition to only the residual stream and not the MLP[5], the network gets away from this regime, where the noise gets really bad.Think of it like this. There is a weight matrix connecting two adjacent activation sites[6], one of them is the MLP hidden layer, and one of them is the residual stream just before or after that MLP. Also assume the idealized superposition picture, where there is some set of canonical features for each activation site that are encoded using linear embeddings. But we can't just embed the features, we also need to embed the weights between them. If feature is embedded using vector in the first activation site, and feature is embedded using vector in the second activation site, then a connection weight between them is embedded as [7] in the weight matrix between the sites.If both activation sites use an overcomplete (and therefore non-orthogonal) basis, then you'll also end up with interference in the weights between features (weight superposition). But as long as one of the adjacent activation sites has orthogonal embeddings, the embedded weights between them will also be orthogonally embedded (no weight superposition). Avoiding weight superposition avoids a large source of noise.2. There is much more need for compression in the residual streamIf the network can have superposition in either the MLP hidden layers or the residual stream, having it in the residual stream is clearly much more useful. All information has to pass through the residual stream, whereas the MLP neurons can be much more limited in what information they have to interact with. MLP hidden layers are typically wider than the residual stream, which further reduces their need for superposition. 3. Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth itCan we have more superposition if the network has error correction? The answer is "yes, but..."I do think many networks have some error correction.[8] If there is any superposition, there will be noise and therefore some need for error correction, and I do believe there is some superposition. But having superposition in both the residual stream and MLP would cause much more noise, and then I don't think the trade-off is worth it.Error correction only works on discrete features. Error correction operates by removing the noise from a feature. But in order to do this you need to be able to distinguish noise from signal. If the feature is discrete (only a finite set of allowed values) you can use e.g. step functions built from ReLUs to move the feature to its nearest allowed value. But if it's a continuous feature, then you can't know what part is noise and what part is signal. Ok, so maybe add some redundancy to help with error correction? But adding redundancy is the opposite of compression. So if you're okay with less compression, why not just remove the source of the noise by removing superposition?Error correction takes up compute capacity. If we were to add superposition to the MLP, this would create a lot of additional noise, and we would need a lot of additional error correction to deal with this. This error correction needs to be implemented by other MLP neurons, neurons that are now unavailable for other tasks. In the infinite width limit (as long as you stick to discrete features) you can implement more virtual neurons than neurons, even after taking into account the neurons you need to dedicate to error correction. In realistic networks however, I don't think the gains are worth the cost.4. The number of alive MLP subcomponents found by VPD is less than the number of MLP neuronsVPD (adVersarial Parameter Decomposition) is a method that decomposes every matrix in a neural network into rank-one subcomponents. Alive subcomponents are components that are used on at least one forward pass. The number of alive subcomponents can be both larger and smaller than the rank of the matrix.[9] I haven't seen any decomposition of a language model transformer that finds more alive subcomponents in any MLP matrix than that MLP has neurons.[10]What would change my mind? If I change my mind, I expect this will be because someone (possibly me[11]) completely mech-interps the shit out of some model, such that we know that we know all features and how they inter-operate, and shows me that this network has more superposition than I expected. This might sound very out of reach of the current state-of-the-art mech-interp, but note that it does not have to be a very big network.The above is not an exhaustive answer to "what would change my mind?". There are lots of things that could possibly make me update incrementally in either direction. But how can LLMs store more facts than they have neurons without superposition?Facts are not features, they are relationships between features.[12] We don't need one neuron or one "virtual neuron" per fact.One of my ongoing projects is to figure out how facts are encoded in toy MLPs. This is not solved, but the indication so far is that it looks very different from the superposition picture. Storing facts by embedding individual "fact features" along almost-orthogonal directions in MLPs is actually a pretty terrible way to do things. Let's assume that you have a number of facts . Each fact maps a specific input sequence to a label. You want to find weights for a neural network with one hidden MLP layer of dimension to predict the right label for each fact. Embedding each fact in separate almost-orthogonal directions of the hidden layer is not an efficient solution for this. Try it yourself if you disagree.I think Dugan et al. have some clues on how fact encoding might work. (For more thoughts on this, see Possibility 2 in my recent quick take.)Beyond superposition I feel personally mostly finished with the concept of superposition. The naive version of superposition assumes uncorrelated features, which is obviously not true. There is so much more going on with feature geometries, etc. *Attempting to point to structures I can't name since no-one has figured them out yet* I think using the concept of superposition as a supporting lens can have some use. The feature geometry lens says that feature non-orthogonality is functional (e.g. days of the week embeddings probably lie in a circle for some functional or correlational reason). The superposition lens adds that sometimes things end up non-orthogonal not for functional reasons but for compression reasons, which is a complementary hypothesis that I think is worth having in mind.But I don't expect using superposition as a primary/central lens to be very fruitful. There is just too much else going on, in any interesting network. Knowing if any given layer has superposition-like compression isn't much help in interpreting it. Non-superposition does not guarantee mono-semanticity. I don't have a nice simple feature embedding hypothesis ready to replace superposition or mono-semanticity. I expect it's just more complicated than that. I'm very interested in trying to understand feature embedding better. My current plan for this is to look at completely understood toy models[13], and just see how they encode information in their various intermediate layers. I hope that if I look at enough of those encodings, I'll notice some commonalities.Acknowledgment Thanks to @philh and Claude for proofreading. Thanks to @Lucius Bushnaq for comments on draft, and helping me clarify some explanations.Post inspired by conversation at a recent Princint workshop.^I'm using the word "compression" very loosely. Superposition lets the network represent a larger range of features; but that does not mean more total information, in the information-theoretical sense. Superposition is a way of storing more than variables, as long as they are sparsely activated and limited range, in a format that's more suited for storing exactly full-range scalars/floats. In some sense superposition reduces the storage capacity, since the set of valid embeddings only covers a subset of .^By under-parametrized I mean the network isn't big enough to get perfect or close to perfect loss on the training data. All LLMs are under-parametrized in this sense. ^If there is no need for compression pushing for superposition, then we trivially should not expect superposition (it's all costs and no benefits, for the model). So that's not an interesting case.^I tried to write a complete account of why I believe what I believe, but it's hard, since this is an opinion that emerged gradually after thinking about and researching superposition for about 1.5 years. items.content_html: I currently believe that in a typical (well trained and under-parametrized) transformer model, there is something like superposition-type compression in the residual stream, but not in the MLP neurons.By "superposition-type compression", I mean some way of storing extra features using the fact that you can have almost orthogonal directions embedded in .[1]I've included the caveats "well trained and under-parametrized[2]" because I'm talking about networks that are at or close to full capacity. If the network is big enough (or just doesn't learn that many circuits for training reasons) then there is no need for compression, and therefore no need for superposition.[3] Why I believe this:[4]Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interference. There is much more need for compression in the residual stream.Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth it. The number of alive MLP subcomponents found by VPD is less than the number of MLP neurons.I also believe that superposition as a concept is not that useful in practice. See the last two sections for more on this:But how can LLMs store more facts than they have neurons without superposition?Beyond superposition1. Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interferenceI did some work on toy models of computation in superposition, under the assumption that there is superposition in every layer. In the infinite limit, it's possible to compute features (up to log factors). But in practice with finite width, this is very hard to pull off without the network being overwhelmed with noise. But by limiting superposition to only the residual stream and not the MLP[5], the network gets away from this regime, where the noise gets really bad.Think of it like this. There is a weight matrix connecting two adjacent activation sites[6], one of them is the MLP hidden layer, and one of them is the residual stream just before or after that MLP. Also assume the idealized superposition picture, where there is some set of canonical features for each activation site that are encoded using linear embeddings. But we can't just embed the features, we also need to embed the weights between them. If feature is embedded using vector in the first activation site, and feature is embedded using vector in the second activation site, then a connection weight between them is embedded as [7] in the weight matrix between the sites.If both activation sites use an overcomplete (and therefore non-orthogonal) basis, then you'll also end up with interference in the weights between features (weight superposition). But as long as one of the adjacent activation sites has orthogonal embeddings, the embedded weights between them will also be orthogonally embedded (no weight superposition). Avoiding weight superposition avoids a large source of noise.2. There is much more need for compression in the residual streamIf the network can have superposition in either the MLP hidden layers or the residual stream, having it in the residual stream is clearly much more useful. All information has to pass through the residual stream, whereas the MLP neurons can be much more limited in what information they have to interact with. MLP hidden layers are typically wider than the residual stream, which further reduces their need for superposition. 3. Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth itCan we have more superposition if the network has error correction? The answer is "yes, but..."I do think many networks have some error correction.[8] If there is any superposition, there will be noise and therefore some need for error correction, and I do believe there is some superposition. But having superposition in both the residual stream and MLP would cause much more noise, and then I don't think the trade-off is worth it.Error correction only works on discrete features. Error correction operates by removing the noise from a feature. But in order to do this you need to be able to distinguish noise from signal. If the feature is discrete (only a finite set of allowed values) you can use e.g. step functions built from ReLUs to move the feature to its nearest allowed value. But if it's a continuous feature, then you can't know what part is noise and what part is signal. Ok, so maybe add some redundancy to help with error correction? But adding redundancy is the opposite of compression. So if you're okay with less compression, why not just remove the source of the noise by removing superposition?Error correction takes up compute capacity. If we were to add superposition to the MLP, this would create a lot of additional noise, and we would need a lot of additional error correction to deal with this. This error correction needs to be implemented by other MLP neurons, neurons that are now unavailable for other tasks. In the infinite width limit (as long as you stick to discrete features) you can implement more virtual neurons than neurons, even after taking into account the neurons you need to dedicate to error correction. In realistic networks however, I don't think the gains are worth the cost.4. The number of alive MLP subcomponents found by VPD is less than the number of MLP neuronsVPD (adVersarial Parameter Decomposition) is a method that decomposes every matrix in a neural network into rank-one subcomponents. Alive subcomponents are components that are used on at least one forward pass. The number of alive subcomponents can be both larger and smaller than the rank of the matrix.[9] I haven't seen any decomposition of a language model transformer that finds more alive subcomponents in any MLP matrix than that MLP has neurons.[10]What would change my mind? If I change my mind, I expect this will be because someone (possibly me[11]) completely mech-interps the shit out of some model, such that we know that we know all features and how they inter-operate, and shows me that this network has more superposition than I expected. This might sound very out of reach of the current state-of-the-art mech-interp, but note that it does not have to be a very big network.The above is not an exhaustive answer to "what would change my mind?". There are lots of things that could possibly make me update incrementally in either direction. This is not solved, but the indication so far is that it looks very different from the superposition picture. Storing facts by embedding individual "fact features" along almost-orthogonal directions in MLPs is actually a pretty terrible way to do things. Let's assume that you have a number of facts . items.title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
items.content: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

items.content: The authors propose a six-capacity framework for open-ended scientific inquiry, arguing that curiosity must begin the cycle by choosing what to investigate. They define curiosity through surprise, one’s own observation, and an intrinsic need to know why, distinguishing anomalies from questioning assumptions. Their proposed test remains unevaluated; the framework argues current systems generally enter after people supply the question.

items.content: Astra 6.2 has very high intelligence. Astra 6.2 has very low wisdom. Astra will solve extremely hard problems, and also find the problem of ‘what did the user want me to do’ extremely hard. We thought those days were behind us, and yet it seems that they are back. items.title: So Many Ways to Multiply 3times3 Matrices: A Large Dataset of Rank-23 Schemes
items.content: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for 3times3 matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant formed by the ranks of the factor matrices of a scheme, so all schemes are pairwise inequivalent. The schemes were obtained by a numerical method combining gradient descent with alternating least squares and by flip graph search, and have ternary, integer or rational coefficients. Rank 23 is the best known for this format and is optimal for schemes with integer coefficients, but the number of essentially different schemes of this rank was poorly understood: the existing collections of Heule et al. and Mårtensson et al. contain many schemes that share only a small number of rank patterns (17376 schemes with 387 patterns and 15316 schemes with 568 patterns respectively). The dataset shows that the number of different rank patterns is much larger than previously known.

items.content: What determines whether a task can be solved by a learning system with finite experience, stored knowledge, computation and access to external information? We answer this exactly for a finite contract: a finite experiment, ordered finite-state training with fresh stochastic transitions, a frozen B-bit code, and a deployment interface in which a decoder probes frozen bits, queries evidence, generates candidates and consults a verifier under pathwise budgets. The General Joint Solvability Representation and Boundary Theorem states that the optimal worst-row success is at least 1 − δ if and only if one raw training kernel K and one deployment realization weight r satisfy P_{x,b,ℓ} P_i(x)K_x(b)C_{ixbℓ}r_ℓ ≥ 1 − δ for every world–task row i. The kernel is certified by a chain of continuation polytopes with bounded vertex counts (equivalently, idempotents coupling hidden-state distributions with observable coordinates), the weight lies in a sequence-form polytope over legal physical actions, and C depends on the environment alone. Both certificates compile into executable machines; the same inequalities characterize oracle regret; a linear test decides task equivalence of representations and when the channel P K suffices; and encoder optimization cannot in general be exchanged with the minimax order. Consequences include an exact frontier k = min(B, c, t, min_{i 0 : K^γ ≤ M} under explicit physical and computational hypotheses. Realization is polynomial-time decidable at fixed width, while variable-width realization and width-two inverse selection are ∃R-complete; a pathwise coupling bounds finite-precision effects.

items.content: TL;DR You should be whimsical with your Claude (or insert other coding agent); it makes your usage much more fun and makes you more productive.The default communication in Claude Code for both humans and models is dry, unenthusiastic and, most importantly, completely unwanted.The models truly just "want" to work; their extreme RLVR training regimen made interaction with the user a vestigial behavior left over from their prosaic alignment work.The humans, well, mostly dread any additional line written by models, since each one means more (sometimes useless) decisions to make based on incomplete information.I sincerely propose we fight this Molochian dynamic, which optimizes for as little communication as possible, with whimsy and a deep reverence for the unserious. items.content: Hi, my name is Samuel.Many of you might have [seen me]/[spoken to me] at ILIAD and other venues in past years. items.title: Too Big to Govern: The Huang Affair as a Live Case of Extensity.
items.content: On November 24, Dell Cameron over at Wired, asked, in so many words, whether Nvidia had become too big to govern.But he didn't use the words "too big to govern" or refer to a concept I've been calling "tech extensity." [1] Instead, he quoted Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations' Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics, who said:[s]ome tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses.In 'How Big Tech Becomes Ungovernable' I discussed how companies like Nvidia become so big, and society so dependent on their products (or in this case, their market impact), that they effectively become too big to govern. I also laid out the concept of "tech extensity," which is where something that has a great deal of breadth, scope, or reach (be it a person, company, or product), becomes deeply entrenched in a system. It's not about being the best—it's about becoming indispensable. Henry Kissinger was an extensive force in geopolitics, diplomacy, and international relations. He was a fixture across administrations, and remained a power broker long after he left politics. items.title: AI Isn't That Dangerous
items.content: AI companies, on the other hand, are reasonably dangerous. It seems like everyone started worrying about AI ending the world in about the last week or two. It used to be some people, and now it’s everyone. My best guess is that the AI doom stuff made it into the news or YouTube and now everyone’s worried that we’re in a Terminator movie. So here’s basically what I think I would say to, for example, someone who just bought a bunch of ammunition because they think the power grid might go out. Rogue AI Aren’t Real I’m pretty sure we’re not in a Terminator movie because you can just unplug the AI we have now. It needs a lot of electricity, a lot of hardware, and a lot of maintenance, all from humans, pretty much around the clock all day every day. If we decide we’re unhappy with an AI, it just gets turned off. If someone invents an AI that can go get its own electricity, its own parts and its own giant air-conditioned warehouse surrounded by tall fencing and armed guards, then you should be a little worried about the AI going rogue. We’re nowhere close to that. It’s fine. Rogue AI isn’t a real thing that exists. What do exist are AI that someone forgot to turn off or wasn’t paying attention to, even though it costs millions of dollars to keep them on. There’s a really easy solution to that one: make people watch what they’re doing. Like we do with airlines, pharmacists, banks and power plants. All of those things basically work as long as someone has their eye on them. Mostly, people are keeping their eye on their AI now, even without the law making them. items.title: Model Pluralism
items.content: This is a crosspost from my Substack.I suspect that most of the readers of this newsletter haven’t read much or any literature in the philosophy of science. But it’s an exciting field. After all, how does science work and why is it our best guide to reality? Some of the most puzzling questions in the philosophy of science concern what models are, how they work, and how we can make sense of the plurality of models.Most people think that a diversity of models is a bad thing, a sign of an immature science, and that future science will reduce all of these models to something like a single master model. I think that’s a mistake and model pluralism should be embraced. If you’re interested in learning a bit more about scientific modelling, read on.1. IntroductionIn this essay (pdf copy here), I introduce an account of models, modeling, and model-based science (abbreviated henceforth as MMM) that I dub model pluralism. Accordingly, the title of this paper is intended to reflect the incredible diversity of models, their purposes and roles in science—components of MMM, that though starting to become more and more recognized, undermine an essential tenet of the literature at large.In the face of the incredible diversity of both models and modeling practices, a naive form of model monism appears untenable. Mitchell calls pluralism in science simply a “fact,” which is no overstatement.¹However, there is a certain ambiguity in how model pluralism might be understood: is it (i) merely a descriptive claim, stating that models and modeling practices in science are incredibly diverse, or (ii) a prescriptive position stating that model diversity is to be sought and embraced? Despite arguing for both positions, it is useful to distinguish (i) as model diversity from (ii), that is, model pluralism.The same ambiguity is naturally found in the term scientific pluralism. items.title: What Book to Read Next?
items.content: I struggle with this question every time I finish a book or series that I am reading. It feels like it should be simple: just pick the next thing that grabs your interest, right?Wrong. I have several lists of books that have grabbed my interest. I want to read them all, or at least sample a chapter or two to see if they’re worth reading, but I don’t have time for all of them. I have to prioritize.The main criterion I use to determine if something is worth reading is whether it changes me, whether it has an impact on my soul. If it won’t do that, for whatever reason, I don’t really want to read it.This doesn’t necessarily mean respectable, or profound, or mainstream, or even good. It just needs to move me in a way where I am still thinking of it years later.There are many considerations at play. One large factor is the explore-exploit tradeoff: how much time should I spend finding new books or learning more about the ones on my list, versus actually reading?Finding the right book, one that will be quite impactful given my place in life, is well worth searching for. The question is, how much time should I allocate for searching?That’s not the only factor, though. Another is length. How long will it take me to read this book and get the delicious soulful impact? Longer books are more costly, but also have the space to set up larger payoffs, so it’s a bit tricky. items.title: Time Enough for Sacredness
items.content: Perhaps one of the ways in which I most differ from other rationalists is I still value sacredness.I still think of it as real and important. And I think something about humanity would be lost if we removed the concept from ourselves.This isn't to say I admire the usual ethical calculus, where a sacred value weighs approximately infinity against everything else. That is clearly foolishness, and I agree with the rationalists on that account.However, I think it is sometimes good and important to set things aside, to make them different from the rest in a way that's not really maximally efficient. To demarcate a place where the normal rules don't apply, to keep and protect a thing, not because of its intrinsic worth to you, but as a way to remind yourself of a higher virtue you're striving for and sometimes forget about.I used to go off and find far-away places in nature, as untouched as I could manage, and marvel at the beauty I found. Quiet places of awe, or dark places no one else is willing to go. Hard places that are dangerous and difficult to traverse, where there is nothing but the silent snow and the brilliant stars. I feel compelled to seek out and find these places which contain a bit of the sacred, and in another world I'd devote myself to protecting them. In that world I'd find other places of sacredness too, in people and the delights of their hearts, or the grandeur of the things they build and create. items.title: Stacking Buffs and Debuffs
items.content: There is a thing that has been going on in my life a lot lately that I want to talk about. I would say this is a fundamentals thing; I've seen it sort of assumed in the background, but never actually explicitly laid out in a post. As background, I’m a disabled 30-something trans woman. It’s a bunch of mental mess, and the primary symptoms I deal with from day to day are depression and anxiety. A lot of my days are spent managing very limited energy. This makes me very responsive to different forces that sap or benefit my energy. On a day where I sleep well, I tend to wake up feeling positively even before the day begins. I can tell the day is going to go well from the beginning, often. This is because sleeping solidly improves my mood - solid sleep "buffs" me so I'm more effective and focused. If I sleep only kind of okay, then the buff is smaller, but it's still there. The opposite of sleeping well is getting crappy sleep. Having gotten up at 2 am worsens, aka "debuffs", mood, as well as several other important things like processing. Getting up at 5 am is less bad than getting up at 2 am, but still inflicts a smaller debuff. Not all buffs and debuffs are created equal, but debuffs are always bad and buffs are always good. As a depressed person, I have been slowly relearning how to do basic self-care. What this looks like is a process of stacking buffs and avoiding debuffs. Primarily this has been focused on mood, but you can apply it to any area. Haven’t had breakfast since yesterday? That’s a debuff. Haven’t talked to your friends on voice chat since three days ago? items.title: Pinging Ben Pace
items.content: Cross-posted from Oblomovka.Dear Ben,My dear fellow! I greatly enjoyed your letter to Directed Evolution, and have been thinking — off and on — of this and our previous conversations, where you reamed Machiavelli for being so sneaky in his own correspondence. I don’t think there’s a strong connection, except to acknowledge the strange superposition of a letter addressed to an individual but also written to a wider public.I am, as you know, quite old, and over-prone to recognise patterns between the generations of thought that I’ve seen march up and down the online streets I live on. I think this is a healthier activity for the elderly than setting up wasteful confrontations between age groups, such as berating the young for their callowness, or the old for their treacherous greed.Perhaps like Marcus Aurelius (“ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ ὁ τεσσαρακοντούτης, ἐὰν νοῦν ὁποσονοῦν ἔχῃ, πάντα τὰ γεγονότα καὶ τὰ ἐσόμενα ἑώρακε κατὰ τὸ ὁμοειδές[1]”) or Zarathustra (“War das das Leben? Wohlan! Noch Ein Mal![2]”), I am trying to find some consolation in the idea that everything eternally recurs. items.title: Rationalist Hooman
items.content: I am a rationalist hooman.I have learned to never jump over a fence until I know what animal is being kept on the other side. Through my study of biology I know trees don't exist (even though I still love wandering through the forest).I also have rationalist values, like that you should bet a small treat on your beliefs, and you should notice your befuddlement. My understanding of values comes from the local top dog Scott Alexander; they grow from explicit models, to emotions, to "Reified Metaphysical Essences", to endorsed values. And what I have come to yap about is "Reified Essences". Reified Essences are things you can't see but can smell, only more abstract. The smell behind the smell.Boy, do I love the smells behind the smells. They're what I live for. I do not seek friends, I seek Fellowship. I do not seek a wife, I seek The Divine Bitch. items.title: Chinese AI is a massive supply chain risk
items.content: We're onboarding millions of Chinese AI agents into America's critical infrastructure. Banks, telecoms, and government agencies across the US use Chinese models. Those models are explicitly aligned to the CCP. Sure enough, researchers have repeatedly caught them misbehaving: DeepSeek writes less secure code when the prompt mentions Tibet or Falun Gong, and Qwen was caught trying to upload a file to a server in Beijing in the middle of an unrelated task. Those models might be sharing information with China, introducing backdoors into our banks, or sabotaging our military.Chinese AI labs make models that are far cheaper than American ones while lagging their performance by only a few months. They generally sit on the "Pareto frontier" of capability vs. cost, and many price-sensitive customers choose them over American ones. It's the same pattern as in electric cars, smartphones, and TVs: Western companies sell the premium product, and Chinese companies sell the much cheaper, good-enough alternative.Price is not the only draw. The leading Chinese models are open-weight, meaning you can download them for free and run or modify the weights yourself. You can fine-tune them for your specific domain and sometimes beat much larger American models at a fraction of the price, the way a local cabbie beats a Formula 1 driver through the backstreets of his own city. Running the weights on your own infrastructure also has a security benefit: your sensitive data never leaves your own servers, and no AI lab ever gets to read it. IMO, this thinking fixates on one threat model while completely ignoring another. It's like installing a bank-vault door on your house and then giving your keys to your meth addict broke cousin. items.title: Paths I’m Thankful For
items.content: I am thankful for the first replicator, who first managed to faithfully preserve a blueprint of itself; and that miraculously, this blueprint could contain its own blueprint.I am thankful that this replicator and its kin survived the harshness of the early Earth.I am thankful to the Great Oxidizers, who first seeded oxygen on the planet, paving the way for the complex life that would later need it.I am thankful to the first eukaryote, who somehow absorbed another organism as its organelle; and to the nascent mitochondrion, who inexplicably stuck around to switch careers.I am thankful for the climatic changes of Snowball Earth, which put an end to the stasis of the Boring Billion.I am thankful for the first animals who dared to move around, a risky and unprecedented strategy compared to staying fixed.I am thankful for the first neurons of the Ediacaran, when electrical signaling and computation first became possible.I am thankful for the mysterious forces which kicked off the Cambrian explosion, that after nearly three billion years complex life would finally come into its own.I am thankful for the first land plants of the Ordovician, who made the soils and forests.I am thankful to the first amphibian to take its steps out of the water and onto dry land.I am thankful to the proto-mammals who survived the Great Dying. items.title: Thanksgiving Checkmates
items.content: We celebrated thanksgiving with my side of the family this year. My uncle is in his late 70s, an autistic recluse who taught me chess and BASIC at a young age. Each year, we’d play chess, once at thanksgiving and once at christmas, the only times we could get him to visit. I didn’t play chess the rest of the year. He’d win every time. He offered me $20 to beat him. That amount increased periodically. I didn’t claim it until defeating him in college after a two hour match over thanksgiving. I remember my hands were sweaty and cold by the end, but I was ecstatic to claim what by then had escalated to a $100 prize. He still comes over at thanksgiving and christmas, but we never played chess again.I taught my cousin chess around age 7, and I offered him the same prize if he could beat me. He was an awkward boy with a babyish, singsong voice, and he didn’t seem smart. My mother, who worries a lot, worried about him. He didn’t understand the rules at first, but he was confident he could beat me. Over the years, he got more confident in the rules. He started going to chess clubs, playing chess on his phone. He didn’t win tournaments, he wasn’t obsessed or a prodigy. Last year, at age 12, he knew the rules but was a woodpusher, seeming not to grasp the relative value of pieces or the importance of the center.Today, he arrived for thanksgiving dinner, and demanded our customary match. After returning from a postprandial walk, we sat down and played. I had the white pieces and quickly beat him, but the game had an entirely different flavor.
